title: Five villages for peace
hook: Sanjaya arrives from the blind king with a message about peace, and Yudhishthira answers with a very small request
carry: karma yoga: holding back isn't holy; act rightly
tomorrow: why does Krishna refuse a royal feast?

segments.voice: Yesterday: Udyoga, the getting ready, began at Krishna's bedside, and Arjuna chose Krishna over an army. Your line was bhakti: want God himself, not just his gifts.

An envoy rides into the Pandava camp. It's Sanjaya, the trusted charioteer and counselor of the blind king Dhritarashtra. He greets everyone warmly, asks after their health, and then delivers his master's message. It isn't an offer. It isn't a threat. It's a plea: don't fight. And something is missing from it. Dhritarashtra asks for peace, but he doesn't offer to give back what was taken.
screen: `SANJAYA RIDES IN.` → `THE MESSAGE: DON'T FIGHT.` → `WHAT THE MESSAGE LEAVES OUT.`

segments.voice: Sanjaya speaks movingly, and the Pandavas don't brush it aside. A war between cousins, he says, means killing your own teachers, your own uncles, your own kin. What kind of victory is that? Better, he says, to live on alms than to win a kingdom that way. Yudhishthira's answer is not angry. I want peace too, he says. Who would choose war if peace were possible? But peace has to mean something. Give us back our own kingdom, Indraprastha, the city we built. Then Krishna speaks, and gently turns the tables. Sanjaya's way sounds holy: give it up, walk away, beg rather than fight. But he's asking only one side to give anything up. And holding back, Krishna says, is no answer by itself. No one lives without acting. Even the gods act; the sun never rests from its work. A person must act, and act rightly. And then, in this same exchange, Yudhishthira makes a request so small it's almost painful to hear. Not the whole kingdom. Not even the city. Give us five villages, he says, and let this end. Five villages, from men who once ruled. Sanjaya carries the message home. Many readers hear in Krishna's reply an early sounding of the Bhagavad Gita, where Krishna teaches karma yoga: don't run from your duty; do it rightly, and offer it to God. It's why so many Hindus treat ordinary work as worship. And Yudhishthira's five villages are karma yoga in action. Not a war cry, and not a shrug: the fairest, smallest act he can make.
screen: `SANJAYA: DON'T FIGHT YOUR KIN` · `KRISHNA: HOLDING BACK ISN'T HOLY` · `GIVE US FIVE VILLAGES` · then, large: `KARMA YOGA: ACT RIGHTLY`

segments.voice: Pick one thing you've been putting off because it's hard: a reply, an apology, a fair ask. Breathing in, see yourself doing it, plainly and kindly. Breathing out, offer it the way many Hindus do before a task: Krishnarpanam astu, may this be an offering to Krishna. If you don't pray, offer it to someone you love.
Udyoga. The getting ready, where an envoy asks for peace, and Yudhishthira asks for five villages.

chat.meaning: Krishna answered Sanjaya that no one lives without acting, and Yudhishthira acted: he said he wanted peace and asked, kindly, for five villages. That's karma yoga: do the right act, don't flee it.
